title: Sudama's handful of rice
hookLine: a poor man brings the richest friend in the world a handful of flattened rice
carry: bhakti: a leaf given with love is enough
last: RAJA-GUHYA — ALL BEINGS REST IN GOD, LIKE WIND IN THE SKY.

lines: A POOR MAN. A KING FOR A FRIEND.
cards: A poor Brahmin, the one later tellings call Sudama, has barely enough to feed his family. As a boy he studied with Krishna. Now Krishna is a king in a golden city, and Sudama's wife begs him to visit his old friend.
But what do you bring a king? He borrows a few handfuls of flattened rice and ties them in a corner of his worn cloth.
At the palace, Krishna runs to hug him, washes his feet, and then notices the little bundle he's trying to hide. What's that you've brought me?

teach.h: A HANDFUL OF RICE, EATEN WITH JOY.
teach.b: In the Bhagavata Purana's telling, Krishna takes the rice and eats it with delight, and he speaks words that are also a verse of the Gita, the one that crowns today's reading: whoever offers me with love a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, I accept that offering of love from the one whose heart is pure.
Gita nine, twenty-six. Patram, pushpam, phalam, toyam. Nothing costly; anyone can find them.
The verses before it build the scene. Krishna says fools look past him in human form, but great souls, verse fourteen says, are always singing about him, bowing, steady in their vows.
He is the ritual and the offering, the fire and the ghee, verse sixteen.
He is the father of the world, verse seventeen; the mother, the grandparent; the goal, the support, the lord, the witness, the home, the refuge, the friend.
Verse twenty-two: to those who worship me alone, always united with me, I bring what they lack and protect what they have.

teach.h: A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.
teach.b: So when the Lord of everything gets to name what he wants, he names a leaf.
Not because the gift is big, but because the love is real.
The word the verse leans on is bhakti: devotion, love turned toward God.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO OFFERS A LEAF.
teach.b: And Sudama, the story says, walked home without having asked for anything, and found his hut had become a palace.

how: In daily puja many Hindus offer flowers, tulsi or bilva leaves, fruit and water at the home shrine; Gita 9.26 is often recited to explain that what matters is the love, not the size of the offering.

o: a costly gift laid at a temple
a vow to give up worldly life

games.q: who and what — tap the pairs.
p: brought a handful of flattened rice

s: the Gita says God accepts only costly offerings
verse 26: a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, offered with love.
in the story, Krishna eats Sudama's rice with delight
he takes the flattened rice from the bundle Sudama was trying to hide.
he went home without asking for anything, and found his home transformed.

games.q: you're Sudama, at the palace of your childhood friend, now a king. all you have is a little flattened rice in your cloth. what do you do?
o: give it proudly, as a king's gift.
sell it to buy something better.
games.why: he tries to hide it, and Krishna finds it and eats it with joy. the gift mattered because of the love, not the price.

practice: Hold something small in your open hands, a glass of water, a leaf, a flower, a piece of fruit, or simply picture one, and think of what you'd offer with it: thanks, a worry, a person you love.
If you pray, you can offer it to God, as the verse says; if not, simply hold it with care, as if it were a gift.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti. Devotion, love turned toward God. Gita nine, twenty-six: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, offered with love, is accepted.

orig.note: Sanskrit: patram pushpam phalam toyam, a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water (Gita 9.26).

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti, a leaf given with love is enough. That's why a home shrine needs no gold, just a flower and some water. Until tomorrow.
